reason: Selected agent-count and recursion sweeps support checking orchestration scale rather than assuming larger teams help.

candidates.title: Sweep agent count and recursion depth before scaling a team
candidates.rule: For long-horizon research or workflow agents, compare a small shallow team with larger or recursively delegated configurations, including aggregate tokens and task quality.
candidates.passage: allowing sub-agents to spawn further sub-agents tends to reduce performance and increase token usage.
candidates.finding: Within SAIGE, the four-agent depth-one default scores best on the two ablated benchmarks; larger pools or deeper recursion generally cost more and score less. Broader comparisons favor single agents on tightly coupled terminal work and teams on some sparse-dependency tasks.
models: SAIGE backbone not established in inspected sections; DeepSeek-V4-Pro is the failure-analysis model
workloads: Terminal Bench 2.1 and NL2Repo main comparisons
candidates.conditions: Vary maximum agents four to six and recursion depth one to three; aggregate input/output traffic across all agents.
candidates.limitations: No inspected repeated-run uncertainty. Task dependence is diagnosed observationally; the sweep does not establish a universal four-agent optimum or that recursive delegation always harms. Token traffic is not complete monetary cost.
candidates.validation_test: Compare single-agent and several shallow/deep team sizes under a measured total budget; stratify by task dependencies and inspect coordination deadlocks, omissions and quality.

review_scope: Selected abstract, introduction, methods or main-result sections; not a comprehensive paper or appendix review.
